questions.q: A file called notes.txt is already there. Read the whole of notes.txt in one go. Close the file. Display exactly what was in it and nothing of your own.

teach.say: open() takes a file name and a mode, and 'r' means read. .read() brings the whole file back as one string, and .close() lets go of it.

questions.starter: # read it all, close it, print it

tests.why: Both lines come out of one .read(). If you only got the first line you used .readline(), which stops after one.
A one-line file reads just as easily. If nothing printed, you read the file into a variable but never printed it.
Three lines, one .read(). If you printed a heading of your own as well, the output will not match - print only the file.

questions.fb: open() needs the file name and the mode. 'r' means read. .read() brings back the whole file as one string, newlines and all, and .close() lets go of it.

questions.q: A file called data.txt is already there, and it may be empty. Read the whole of data.txt. Count every character in it, newlines included. Display characters [the count] and nothing else.
brief: One space after the word characters.

tests.why: Three letters and the newline on the end make 4. If you got 3 you stripped the newline off, and the question says to count it.
An empty file is still a file. .read() gives back an empty string, so the length is 0 - a program that crashes or prints nothing here assumed there would always be something to read.
Five characters, a newline, six characters, a newline is 13. If you got 11 you counted the lines separately and lost the newlines.
The last line of a file does not have to end with a newline. If this gave 2 you are adding one on yourself.

questions.fb: len() on what .read() gave back counts the characters in the whole file. Newlines are real characters, which is why a file usually looks longer than you expect.

questions.q: A file called words.txt is already there, and it may be empty. Read the first line of words.txt only. Close the file. Strip the newline off that line. Display first [that line]. Then display length [how many characters are left] on the next line.

teach.say: .readline() reads up to the next newline only, so what comes back still has \n on the end. .strip() takes it off.

brief: An empty file has no first line, so the word first is printed on its own.
questions.starter: # one line only, then strip it

tests.why: Only the first line is wanted, and copper lane is 11 characters. If slate row appeared too you used .read() or .readlines() instead of .readline().
A file with one line in it. A length of 5 means the newline is still counted, so the line was never stripped.
An empty file gives .readline() an empty string back, not an error. A program that crashes here assumed there is always a first line to read.
The first line of a longer file is still just the first line. If a blank line appeared between the two outputs, the newline is still stuck on the end of what you printed.

questions.fb: .readline() reads up to and including the next newline, so what comes back has \n on the end. .strip() takes that off, along with any stray spaces, and the length shows whether it really went.

questions.q: A file called words.txt is already there, with one word per line, and it may be empty. Read words.txt. Count how many lines it holds. Display lines [that count] and nothing else.
questions.starter: # how many lines are in there

tests.why: Three words, so three lines. If the count was 20 you counted characters rather than lines.
One word is one line. A count of 0 means .readlines() was called after the file had already been read to the end.
An empty file gives .readlines() an empty list, so the count is 0 - and that 0 still has to be printed.
Four lines. If you got 1, you read the file with .read() and counted the one long string it gave back.

questions.fb: .readlines() gives you a list with one string per line, so len() on that list tells you how many lines the file holds.

questions.q: A file called words.txt is already there, with one word per line, and it may be empty. Read words.txt. Display one line for each word, in the form [position] [word], counting the positions from 1. Display none instead, on a line of its own, when the file holds no words.
brief: Strip each word's newline before printing it.

tests.why: Three words, numbered from 1. If your numbers ran 0 1 2 you used the list position straight, and the question asks you to start at 1.
One word is one line, numbered 1.
An empty file gives .readlines() an empty list, so the loop simply does not run and the one word none is printed instead. A crash here means you went straight for lines[0] without checking.
If each word printed with a blank line after it, the newline from the file is still attached - strip it before printing.

questions.fb: Each string .readlines() gives you still ends with \n until you strip it, and the position you print is the list position plus 1.

questions.q: Ask the user for a word. Make a file called out.txt. Write that word into out.txt on one line. Write ready on the next line. Close the file. Then read out.txt back in one go. Display what you read.

teach.say: Mode 'w' opens a file for writing, making it if it is not there. .write() adds no newline of its own, so you put the \n in yourself.

brief: There is no out.txt to start with, so the program creates it.
.write() adds no newline of its own.
questions.starter: # write it, close it, read it back

tests.why: The file has to exist before you can read it back. A crash saying no such file means the write never happened, or you opened the wrong name.
The word comes from input, the word ready is fixed. If both ended up on one line you forgot the \n after the word - .write() adds nothing of its own.
If the output was empty, you read the file before closing it after writing - what you wrote may still be waiting to be saved.

questions.fb: print() puts a newline on the end for you. .write() does not, so you have to write \n yourself when you want a new line in the file.

questions.q: Ask the user for a word. Open the file data.txt in write mode, which empties whatever it held. Write that word into data.txt on a line of its own. Close the file. Then read data.txt back. Display [every line in it], one on each line. Then display lines [how many] on the last line.
brief: data.txt is already there and may already hold lines.
Strip each line's newline before printing it.
questions.starter: # write mode, then count what survived

tests.why: The two old lines are gone, because write mode empties the file first. If you still see slate you opened it with 'a' instead of 'w'.
Writing to an empty file works the same way. If the count said 0 you read the file before closing it.
Three old lines, still only one left. A count of 4 means the new word was added to the end rather than replacing the file.
Writing the same text that was already there still leaves one line, not two.

questions.fb: Opening a file with 'w' empties it the moment it opens, even if you then write nothing. That is the difference between 'w' and 'a', and it is easy to lose work to.

questions.q: Ask the user for a word. Add that word to the end of the file log.txt, on a line of its own. Keep the lines log.txt already holds. Then read the whole of log.txt back. Display [every line in it], one on each line, and nothing else.

teach.say: Mode 'a' appends: it opens the file with the writing point already at the end, so nothing already in there is thrown away.

brief: log.txt is already there and may be empty.
Strip each line's newline before printing it.
The word just added is the last line.
questions.starter: # add to the end, then print the whole file

tests.why: Two lines were there, so three come back. If only moss printed you opened the file with 'w', which wiped copper and slate.
Append mode works on an empty file too, so the one word you added is the whole file.
The new word goes on the end, after glass. Printing lantern first means you wrote before the line that was already there.
If a blank line appeared after each line, the newline is still attached - strip it before printing.

questions.fb: 'a' for append opens the file with the writing point already at the end, so what you write is added. 'w' would throw the whole file away first.

questions.q: Ask the user for a word. Append that word to the file log.txt, on a line of its own. Keep the lines log.txt already holds. Then read the whole of log.txt back. Display latest [the last line]. Then display total [how many lines] on the next line.
brief: log.txt is already there and may be empty.
Strip the newline off the last line before printing it.
questions.starter: # add to the end, then report on the whole file

tests.why: Two lines were there, so adding one makes three. A total of 1 means you opened the file with 'w', which wiped copper and slate.
Append mode works on an empty file too, and the one word you added is also the last line. A crash here means you went for lines[1] rather than the end of the list.
The new word goes on the end, so the last line is the one just added, not glass. Printing glass means you took lines[0].
If a blank line appeared between the two lines of output, the newline is still on the end of the line you read - strip it before printing.

questions.fb: The last line of a file is the last item of the list .readlines() gave you, and len() of that same list is how many lines there are.

questions.q: A file called data.txt is already there, holding one word,number record per line, and it may be empty. Read data.txt. Display one line for each record, in the form [word] [number]. Display none instead, on a line of its own, when the file holds no records.

teach.say: A record is one line made of fields. Strip the newline first, then .split(',') breaks the line into a list of those fields.

brief: One space between the two fields, in place of the comma.
questions.starter: # one record per line, two fields on each

tests.why: Three records, each split into two fields. A comma still in the output means the line was printed as it stood rather than split.
A single record still has to be split. If the number came out with a blank line after it, you split the line before stripping it, so the newline is still part of the second field.
No records at all, so the loop never runs and the one word none is printed instead. A crash here means you read a record before checking there was one.
The fields are printed exactly as the file holds them, so a number of 0 prints as 0.

questions.fb: A record is one line made of fields. .split(',') breaks the line into a list of those fields, so fields[0] is the word and fields[1] is the number.

questions.q: Ask the user for a word to find. The file data.txt is already there, holding one word,number record per line. Look at every record in data.txt. Display [word] is [its number] when a record matches. Display no record instead when none matches. Then display checked [how many records you looked at] on the next line.
brief: Look at every record, even after one has matched.
questions.starter: # one record per line, one word to find

tests.why: slate is the second record, and all three were looked at. If a blank line appeared before the checked line, you split the record before stripping it, so the newline is still part of the number field.
Nothing matches, so the message is printed once after the loop. Printing it three times means the message sits inside the loop instead of after it.
An empty file has no records, so nothing matches and nothing was looked at. A crash here means you read a record before checking there was one.
A file with a single record still has to be searched. If nothing was found, the loop may be stopping before it looks at the only line.
The last record must be checked too. Printing no record here means the loop gave up as soon as the first line failed to match.

questions.fb: Searching a file of records is a linear search over the lines: split each one, compare the field you care about, and only decide what to print once the loop has finished.

questions.q: A file called data.txt is already there, holding one word,number record per line, and it may be empty. Read data.txt. Display no records when it holds none. Otherwise add up every number. Find the word on the record with the highest number. Display total [the numbers added up]. Then display best [that word] on the next line.
brief: The earlier record wins a tie for the highest number.
questions.starter: # the total and the best of one field

tests.why: 7 plus 9 plus 4 is 20, and slate's 9 is the highest. A total of 794 means the number field was joined as text instead of turned into a number with int().
One record is its own total and its own best. If the best came out blank, the highest is only being updated when a later number beats a starting value you never set.
No records at all. A program that prints total 0 here, or crashes looking for the highest, assumed the file always has data in it.
A tie goes to the first one in the file, so the test for the highest has to be strictly greater than, not greater than or equal to.
Numbers of zero are still records. If best came out blank, you started the highest at 0 and nothing ever beat it - start from the first record instead.

questions.fb: Totalling a field means reading each record, pulling out that field, turning it into a number and adding it on. The running total starts at 0 before the loop, never inside it.

questions.q: A file called data.txt is already there, holding one word,first,second record per line, and it may be empty. Read data.txt. Make a file called out.txt. Write a line of [word] [the first number times the second] into out.txt for each record. Then write total [all those values added up] on the last line. Close out.txt. Then read out.txt back. Display the whole of it.

teach.say: One file can be open for reading while another is open for writing, which is how one file is built out of another.

brief: There is no out.txt to start with, so the program creates it.
The total line is written last, after every record's line.
questions.starter: # one file in, another out, then read it back

tests.why: 3 times 50 is 150, 2 times 120 is 240, and the two make 390. If the total line came first, it was written before the loop rather than after.
One record, so its value is also the total. Two identical numbers is right here - do not skip the total line just because it matches.
No records, so nothing is written for them, but the total line still has to be written. A program that writes nothing and then reads an empty out.txt prints nothing at all.
The records must come out in the order they were in the file. If the values were right but the total was 0, the running total is being reset inside the loop.
A first number of zero is worth zero, and the record still gets a line of its own in out.txt.

questions.fb: Reading one file and writing another is the usual shape of this job. Only what you print is seen, so reading out.txt back is how you prove you really wrote it.

questions.q: Ask the user for a limit. The file data.txt is already there, holding one word,number record per line. Read data.txt. Make a file called picked.txt. Write a line of [word] [number] into picked.txt for each record whose number is above the limit. Then read picked.txt back. Display [every line in it], one on each line. Then display picked [how many] on the last line.
brief: The limit is a whole number.
Make picked.txt even when nothing matches.
A number equal to the limit does not count.
One space between the two fields of a line, in place of the comma.
questions.starter: # pick some out, then read the new file back

tests.why: 35 and 28 are both over 25, and copper's 20 is not. If copper appeared too, the numbers are being compared as text - '20' is bigger than '2' as text, so int() is needed.
Nothing is over 50, so picked.txt is written empty and the count is 0. A crash here means you tried to read a file you only opened when there was something to put in it - open it either way.
No records at all, so nothing is picked. The count line still has to be printed.
41 is above 40 by one. If this was missed you used >= on the wrong side, or compared the limit to the word instead of the number.
Exactly the limit is not above the limit, so nothing is written. This is the boundary - >= instead of > fails only here.
Two separate records can hold the same number and both count. If only one line printed, you stopped the loop at the first match.

questions.fb: This is the whole pattern in one program: read records in, decide about each one, write the chosen ones out, then read the new file back. Opening picked.txt before the loop is what makes the empty case work.
